title: Lightweight return-mapping surrogates for multiscale plasticity: a practical guide
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a practical guide to building lightweight neural-network surrogates for the plastic return-mapping process in concurrent multiscale (FE 2 ) simulations. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we show how a deliberately simple feed-forward network, structured to mirror the classical return-mapping update, can replace the prohibitively expensive nested fine-scale solves that dominate the cost of conventional FE 2 schemes based on FFT homogenization at the meso-scale. We walk through the full workflow: generating training data from incremental homogenization analyses, constructing a compact yet sufficient dataset, embedding material symmetries directly into the mapping, and deploying the trained network as a user-defined material subroutine (UMAT) in a standard finite-element solver—enabling widespread use. A sensitivity study examines the model’s robustness to data density, increment size, and mesh refinement, and we characterize the regimes in which the surrogate holds and where it breaks down. For the macroscopically isotropic, two-dimensional plane-stress setting considered here, the surrogate reproduces the reference response while reducing the per-analysis cost from hours to seconds with speed-ups up to 30,000 over standard FE 2 . Moreover, by eliminating the need to store and update the extensive microscale state variables, it drastically reduces memory requirements and enables substantially finer finite element discretizations that would otherwise be impossible. The approach extends naturally to three dimensions and to weaker symmetry assumptions, given an appropriate sampling strategy and dataset.

title: Hyperelastic constitutive model discovery with differentiable finite elements and structure-preserving neural networks
abstract: Abstract The discovery of constitutive laws from experimentally accessible measurements is a central problem in nonlinear computational mechanics. Many data-driven constitutive identification approaches rely either on paired strain–stress data or on full-field displacement measurements, both of which are difficult to obtain in realistic three-dimensional settings. We present a differentiable finite element framework for the discovery of hyperelastic material laws from partial observations, including boundary-only displacement measurements and global reaction forces. The method embeds the nonlinear finite element equilibrium problem directly into the learning loop, so that candidate strain-energy densities are assessed through the deformation fields and reactions they induce. This formulation enforces mechanical equilibrium as a constraint and allows the loss function to be evaluated only at observed locations. To ensure physical admissibility and promote numerical solvability throughout training, the constitutive response is represented by Hyperelastic Neural Networks, a structure-preserving neural class that enforces residual energy and stress-free conditions, frame indifference, isotropic material symmetry, polyconvexity, coercivity, and controlled volumetric growth by construction. The resulting PDE-constrained learning problem is solved using a quasi-Newton strategy combined with continuation and solver-aware backtracking. Numerical experiments in two- and three-dimensional finite elasticity demonstrate accurate recovery of hyperelastic isotropic responses from boundary-only data, robustness to measurement noise, and generalization across geometries, loading conditions, and boundary conditions.

title: On the complementary roles of anisotropic crack density and anisotropic crack driving force in phase-field modeling of mixed-mode fracture
abstract: Phase-field models for anisotropic fracture employ two complementary mechanisms: (i) the anisotropic crack density function, controlling direction-dependent fracture resistance, and (ii) the anisotropic strain energy, governing the fracture driving force. Although the unified framework was presented in Pranavi et al.[Comput. Mech., 73 (2024)], the distinct roles of these mechanisms and their interaction remain uninvestigated. This work addresses this gap by first validating the formulation against mixed-mode fracture experiments on a soft elastomer (Lu et al. [Extreme Mech. Lett., 48 (2021)]), and then conducting systematic parametric studies on single-edge-notched (SEN) and open-hole tension (OHT) specimens to isolate each mechanism. The SEN studies show that the crack density anisotropy controls the crack path and toughness while leaving the elastic response unchanged, whereas the anisotropic strain energy deflects the crack but saturates rapidly. The OHT studies reveal a geometry-dependent role expansion: the anisotropic strain energy governs fiber-orientation-dependent stiffness, peak force, and fracture displacement. When both mechanisms act together, the combined response exhibits nonlinear synergistic interaction exceeding the linear sum of the individual contributions. These results establish that the crack density anisotropy governs the crack path (fracture resistance), while the anisotropic strain energy governs the driving force and, in stress-concentration geometries, additionally controls the elastic strain energy distribution around the stress concentrator.

title: Nonlinear path-following via the asymptotic numerical method on a quantum processor
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising avenue for advancing computational methods in science and engineering. In this work, we introduce the quantum asymptotic numerical method (qANM), a framework for solving nonlinear path-following problems using quantum computing. Based on the principle of high-order perturbation techniques, the proposed method uses Taylor series expansions to transform complex nonlinear systems into sequences of linear equations, which are then solved using quantum linear solvers. The central objective of this study is to demonstrate nonlinear path-following with the required linear systems solved on real quantum hardware. To realize this objective, we develop the quantum-enhanced Jacobi method (q-Jacobi), an iterative quantum linear solver used in the hardware experiment. Numerical simulations on a quantum simulator validate the convergence of the method. A highlight of this work is a proof-of-principle experiment on a superconducting quantum processor. Despite the noise inherent in near-term quantum hardware, the experiment achieves 98% accuracy in tracking the nonlinear solution path. We believe this work provides a useful reference for applying quantum computing to nonlinear computational mechanics.

title: Elastoplastic damage analysis of shells with algebraic derivation of consistent tangent matrix and pseudo-stress
abstract: In this study, an algebraically derived consistent tangent matrix and a pseudo-stress for the local residual are applied to elastoplastic problems with damage for shells. The authors define a coupled problem of the global equation, which denotes the weak form of the equilibrium equation for the overall structure, and the local equation, which represents the constraint condition satisfied at each material point. To solve the coupled boundary value problems, the consistent tangent matrix and the pseudo-stress are constructed algebraically by block Newton method. The proposed scheme does not involve any local iterative calculations and allows us to decrease the residuals of the coupled problem simultaneously, since the pseudo-stress for the local residual is incorporated into the linearized global equation. Some numerical examples using shell elements demonstrate the validity and effectiveness of the proposed approach in complex situations with material and geometrical nonlinearities, including the Lemaitre ductile damage model.

title: From legacy finite element modeling to explainable simulation: Technical requirements for XAI in computational mechanics
abstract: Abstract This paper establishes technical requirements for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in computational mechanics, with an emphasis on controlling both the model-form and discretization errors in finite element analysis. We argue that explanation accuracy and the identification of knowledge limits—central requirements of XAI—can be satisfied only when these error sources are systematically estimated and controlled. A model-centric framework is developed in which hierarchical discretization and model hierarchies enable traceability of modeling assumptions and quantitative assessment of their impact on quantities of interest. The approach is illustrated through numerical studies of the stability and post-buckling behavior of spherical and hemispherical shells. The results indicate that achieving XAI in engineering requires a transition from legacy element-centric implementations to formulations grounded in the science of finite element analysis, with important implications for software architecture and simulation workflows.

title: Controlling normal energy dissipation in energy-conserving contact models for non-spherical particles: energy–phase harmonisation and adaptive damping
abstract: A computational methodology is developed for controlling normal energy dissipation in non-spherical particle contact within the energy-conserving contact (ECC) framework. A key theoretical development is an exact energy–phase transformation for a dynamically closed scalar contact mode. For any monotone contact potential, an energy coordinate together with an intrinsic reparametrisation of time harmonises the nonlinear conservative dynamics into a linear harmonic oscillator. Requiring the transformed damped dynamics to retain the constant-coefficient spring–dashpot form then yields a universal damping law and an exact, impact-velocity-independent restitution calibration for the closed scalar mode. For multidimensional non-spherical contact, the scalar law is evaluated on the instantaneous projected normal state supplied by instantaneous contact dynamics (ICD). This gives an adaptive Rayleigh damping coefficient based on the current projected normal mass and energy-equivalent stiffness. The construction preserves the local force–energy structure of the conservative law, while recognising that the realised response of a fully coupled impact remains configuration- and trajectory-dependent. For the contact-volume formulation (Model I), the conservative interaction is expressed as a contact force–moment pair. Its admissible contact line eliminates the transverse moment, but a residual torsional moment about the contact normal generally remains. The corresponding contact kinematic identity is corrected to include both normal closure and relative spin, enabling the overlap volume to be maintained dynamically without repeated volumetric reconstruction. For multi-patch contact, the additive structure of Model I further leads to a topology-invariant macro-damping formulation in which normal damping is evaluated at the combined-contact level. Smooth-shape benchmarks show that aligned closed-mode impacts recover the prescribed restitution with near-exact accuracy. In coupled impacts, the target-energy fraction \(E_{\text {target}}\) provides a more stable comparative diagnostic than the direct entry–exit velocity ratio. Its near constancy across the prescribed restitution range, observed for many tested configurations, indicates a consistent global dissipation response rather than exact event-level restitution control. Tests with irregular and non-convex triangulated particles further demonstrate robust application under evolving multi-patch contact and strong translation–rotation exchange.

title: 3D concave polyhedral elements for elasticity problem using cell-based smoothed finite element method
abstract: This work presents, for the first time, an extension of the smoothed finite element method to arbitrarily complex discretization for solving elasticity problems, seamlessly incorporating hexahedral, convex, and notably concave polyhedral elements. Concave corners, the mesh distortion that usually occurs in large deformation, is one of the most formidable challenges in computational solid mechanics. To discretize continua using arbitrarily complex concave polyhedral elements with random characteristics, an image-based method that leverages coordinate mapping theory within the FEM framework is proposed to construct these elements. A novel free-Jacobian cell-based smoothed finite element method is formulated for mechanical problems discretized by arbitrarily complex polyhedral elements, yielding superior characteristics in terms of stability, robustness, and resistance to mesh distortion. The Delaunay tetrahedralization algorithm is utilized to automatically generate smoothing domains for polyhedral elements without introducing any virtual nodes. By gradient smoothing techniques, the element-based volume integration is transformed into a series of boundary surface integrals over the smoothing domains, which not only relaxes the continuity requirements for shape functions but also achieves self-stability without the need for additional stabilization terms. Simple benchmark tests and complex engineering examples demonstrate the applicability and robustness of the proposed method in handling non-convex polyhedral meshes.

title: Conforming/nonconforming virtual elements and application to elasticity problems in curved three-dimensional domains
abstract: Abstract The virtual element method (VEM) is a well-established framework for solving partial differential equations on polygonal and polyhedral meshes. In this paper, we introduce a novel hybrid VEM that integrates both conforming and nonconforming virtual spaces. We apply this formulation to a three-dimensional linear elasticity problem, providing rigorous theoretical analysis to demonstrate optimal convergence rates. Furthermore, we extend this approach to domains with curved boundaries, where it naturally provides an exact geometric representation without requiring any structural modifications to the scheme.

title: An advanced finite element–AI coupled framework for high–fidelity and efficient prediction of residual stresses and distortions in laser powder bed fusion
abstract: This research introduces a methodology to estimate inherent strains (IS) in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process by combining a high-fidelity, experimentally-validated finite element (FE) model with machine learning (ML) techniques. The main objective is to enhance computational efficiency in the non-linear coupled thermo-mechanical simulations and thus accelerate the prediction of residual stresses and consequently distortions for part-scale components. The FE model leverages the modified IS approach at the mesoscale. Five ML models are effectively used to efficiently predict simulation data. A comprehensive set of key independent variables was identified and used to train the ML models, including key LPBF processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, hatching space, and scanning strategy), build-height nodal coordinate and nodal temperatures extracted from FE thermal simulations. To enhance the applicability of the developed surrogate ML models, three commonly used nickel-based superalloys were selected to enable generalization across different material types. Among all the developed ML models, categorical boosting (CatBoost), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and optimized KNN exhibited the highest predictive performance for inherent strains in the longitudinal, transverse, and layer-thickness directions, with respective relative errors of 16.5%, 16.3%, and 22.5% compared to FE results. The proposed ML–FE approach accelerates computation by up to 10,000× compared to traditional FE methods while maintaining distortion prediction errors below 16% for cantilever beam geometries. This framework highlights how data-driven modeling can significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of physics-based simulations in metal additive manufacturing, paving the way for rapid process parameter optimization.

title: Correction: The shifted boundary collocation immersogeometric method: an application to Poisson problems
Sensitivity of blast responses in a reinforced concrete slab to damage evolution parameters
abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of blast-induced damage in reinforced concrete (RC) structures requires constitutive models that offer transparent control over softening behavior. This study develops a user-defined material (UMAT) subroutine that extends the built-in concrete damage model in commercial finite element software by exposing four key brittle damage parameters: the evolution rate ( $$A_b$$ A b ), shape ( $$B_b$$ B b ), saturation limit ( $$d_{\max }$$ d max ), and deletion threshold ( $$d_{\textrm{th}}$$ d th ), of which the latter two are internally fixed and inaccessible in the built-in implementation. Numerical simulations of an RC slab under near-field blast loading are validated against experimental midspan deflection and observed cracking patterns. A structured parametric study, varying each parameter independently, reveals that although all configurations can yield similar peak deflection magnitudes, they produce markedly different peak response times and fracture morphologies. Specifically, $$A_b$$ A b governs the rate of stiffness degradation; $$B_b$$ B b controls the curvature of the damage evolution function; $$d_{\max }$$ d max sets the saturation level of strength reduction; and $$d_{\textrm{th}}$$ d th critically advances the peak response time by triggering early element erosion. These distinctions highlight that global deflection alone is insufficient to characterize structural behavior under blast loading, and that physically meaningful control over damage evolution parameters is essential for reliable failure prediction and blast-resistance assessment.

title: Parametric phase-field brittle fracture computations with convolutional Fourier neural operators
abstract: Abstract The variational phase-field approach to fracture has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling complex fracture phenomena, yet in the computational setting its reliance on discretizations that resolve small length scales makes it very expensive for parametric studies and real-time applications. In this paper, we propose the use of the Convolutional Fourier neural operator (C-FNO)—a data-driven operator learning architecture that enhances the global spectral capabilities of Fourier neural operators (FNOs) with local spatial convolutions—to surrogate phase-field brittle fracture simulations. We evaluate the performance of the C-FNO on two-dimensional single-edge notched specimens under varying geometric (initial notch length) and loading (magnitude and angle) parameters. Our results demonstrate that the C-FNO accurately predicts crack propagation, kinking, and branching across unseen parameter combinations, achieving very low mean absolute errors with a training time of a few hours and an inference time of the order of ten seconds. Notably, the addition of local convolution layers allows the model to capture nearly sharp cracks that are typically smoothed out by vanilla FNOs. This work highlights the potential of operator learning frameworks to provide high-fidelity, high-speed predictions for computational fracture mechanics.

title: A discontinuous SPH approach for simulating blast-induced rock fracture and multi-material interaction
abstract: Blast-induced rock fracture is a critical challenge in mining, geotechnical, and defense engineering, involving complex dynamic processes such as high-strain-rate deformation, fragmentation, and multi-material interaction. This paper presents a novel computational framework based on a discontinuous Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach to simulate crack propagation and damage in rock under blast loading. The framework integrates the Grady–Kipp model for tensile damage and the Drucker–Prager criterion for shear failure. Fracture is explicitly modeled using a pseudo-spring crack treatment, while a robust multi-material contact algorithm handles interfacial forces under compression. The implementation is rigorously validated through four benchmark cases: three-dimensional crack branching, a uniaxial compression test, frictional block-sliding, and unconfined compression of cylindrical specimens. The framework is further applied to simulate explosive detonation in a cylindrical rock sample, blast damage near empty holes, and rock blasting with multiple boreholes. These simulations help to understand damage mechanisms under varied initial conditions. The predicted damage patterns and fragmentation results show strong agreement with available experimental data, demonstrating the method’s capability to accurately capture dynamic fracture and complex blast-induced failure in rock.

title: Optimal design of perforated plates
abstract: This study presents a structural optimization framework for silicon nanopore membranes used in bioartificial kidneys. While micromachined slit-pores are essential for blood filtration, they significantly reduce the membrane’s structural stiffness. To maximize rigidity for a fixed total pore area, we optimize the distribution of slit heights across the membrane. Due to the high number of pores ( \(\approx 10^5\) in the membrane), direct numerical simulation is computationally prohibitive. We therefore apply homogenization theory and for a given hole height derive an approximate homogeneous anisotropic plate model. For the obtained effective elasticity tensor, using linear least squares, we determine a smooth surrogate model. This approach transforms the complicated geometry optimization problem into a smooth parametric optimization problem. Then, using the finite element method in a gradient descent algorithm, we minimize two objective functions: the structural compliance and the maximum displacement. This yields, in each case, the optimal distribution of holes of different heights in the perforated membrane. The results provide an efficient computational strategy for designing mechanically robust, high-performance filtration membranes.

title: Design for additive manufacturing: simultaneous optimization of structural integrity and minimal support structures using SIMP
abstract: In additive manufacturing of topology optimized designs, support structures represent a significant challenge, leading to substantial material waste, prolonged build times, and intensive post-processing requirements. This study introduces a sequential three-stage optimization framework aimed at achieving support-free designs by concurrently optimizing structural performance and minimizing the overhang perimeter. The proposed methodology encompasses the generation of an initial freeform design, followed by the determination of an optimal build direction, and culminating in a constrained overhang-perimeter optimization. A primary contribution of this work is the extension of the framework to incorporate stress-based topology optimization alongside compliance-based optimization, enabling support-free, additively manufacturable designs through print-orientation optimization. To ensure manufacturability, a robust formulation and relatively large filter radius are utilized to mitigate the formation of unprintable hanging features. Validated through numerical examples and physical 3D prints, the approach demonstrates that support-free designs are achievable with modest performance trade-offs.

title: A new, simple, and effective variationally consistent mixed finite element formulation for the geometrically exact planar analysis of beams and frames
abstract: A robust and efficient mixed finite element formulation, applicable to both shear-rigid (Kirchhoff-type) and shear-flexible (Reissner-type) beam theories, is proposed for the geometrically exact planar analysis of beams and frames. The formulation is derived from a Hellinger–Reissner-type variational principle, in which the spatial components of the internal forces, bending moment, and cross-sectional rotation are adopted as primary unknowns. Equilibrium of the spatial internal forces is satisfied in strong form at the member level, while the assumed bending moment field is \(C^0\) -continuous and satisfies equilibrium boundary conditions. The formulation is intrinsically free from shear- and membrane-locking phenomena, admits explicit closed-form expressions for both the residual vector and the consistent symmetric tangent matrix, and yields a highly sparse and banded global system with a reduced number of unknowns compared with conventional displacement-based formulations and previously proposed hybrid-mixed formulations. Displacement fields are recovered a posteriori by integrating the kinematic compatibility relations, producing globally \(C^0\) -continuous fields that satisfy all prescribed kinematic boundary conditions. Nonlinear equilibrium paths are traced using an arc-length strategy with a linear extrapolation predictor, and critical points are identified through the determinant of a Schur-complement-based equivalent stiffness matrix that emerges naturally from the formulation. Numerical examples demonstrate the accuracy, convergence, and robustness of the proposed approach, including verification against analytical solutions under pure bending, assessment of shear-locking performance, and the simulation of complex nonlinear responses involving snap-through, snap-back, and symmetry-breaking bifurcation phenomena.

title: A novel variationally consistent nodal integration method based on quadrature weight correction for meshfree reproducing kernel particle method
abstract: Accurate and stable nodal quadrature remains a major challenge in Galerkin meshfree methods, such as the reproducing kernel particle method (RKPM), due to the rational form of the approximation and the need to satisfy variational consistency. This study proposes a novel generalized nodal quadrature rule, termed VCI-w, which optimizes quadrature weights subject to integration constraints, geometric moment constraints, and positivity conditions. The optimized weights are shown to recover optimal convergence rates and provide robust numerical stability by effectively suppressing spurious low-energy oscillatory modes. Unlike geometric smoothing approaches that rely on conforming domains, VCI-w eliminates the dependency on background meshes and preserves the fully meshfree nature of the formulation. In contrast to gradient-modified variationally consistent integration methods that lead to a Petrov–Galerkin structure, VCI-w retains the Bubnov–Galerkin framework, preserving the symmetry of the discrete system. Numerical examples demonstrate optimal or near-optimal convergence across different basis orders, along with improved robustness in both 2D and 3D problems.

title: A shell-in-shell homogenization approach for internally resolved structures
abstract: Abstract In this work we introduce a numerical framework for a multiscale shell-in-shell homogenization. It represents internally resolved shell structures, where on both scales structural shell elements are employed. In contrast to classical shell homogenization strategies, which employ shell elements with displacement degrees of freedom, the present approach considers additionally rotational degrees of freedom. A central novelty is the development of periodic boundary conditions enriched with rotational degrees of freedom so that representative volume elements (RVEs) may contain shell intersections or lack a continuous thickness. In addition, an internal constraint, the so-called moment reduction constraint, and its associated finite element formulation are introduced to ensure that the effective stiffness is independent of the size of the RVE. Furthermore, integration by parts techniques are employed to eliminate rigid body motions and rotations. The proposed approach is validated through linear-elastic benchmark tests. Several linear examples, including corrugated plates and honeycomb structures, are analyzed and compared with corresponding three-dimensional reference solutions.

title: A primal–dual active set framework for adhesive contact of structured interfaces with arbitrary tip geometry, roughness, and buckling
abstract: Structured fibrillar adhesives exhibit contact responses governed by the coupled effects of surface roughness, tip geometry, load redistribution, and structural instability. While increasing preload enhances contact, it can trigger fibril buckling, leading to a catastrophic loss of adhesive capacity—a trade-off difficult to capture with existing computational tools. This study addresses the limitations of traditional lumped models, which fail to resolve intra-fibril contact heterogeneity, by presenting a computationally efficient primal–dual active set (PDAS) framework. The formulation simulates adhesive contact for arbitrary tip geometries and stochastic rough counter-surfaces by discretizing each fibril tip into nodal degrees of freedom. This enables the resolution of partial contact, localized detachment, and heterogeneous traction within an individual fibril footprint. Local axial stiffness is assigned through nodal tip height, while a Laplacian-based coupling operator replicates the lateral load redistribution characteristic of continuum mechanics. Adhesive interaction is modeled using a bounded nodal tensile-force condition, and buckling-induced adhesion loss is incorporated through a history-dependent degradation law. The resulting constrained contact problem is solved using a PDAS strategy based on both primal nonpenetration and dual force-admissibility conditions. Verification confirms discretization convergence and consistency with Hertzian scaling, while simulations of spherical-cap, wedge-shaped, and periodic tips reproduce geometry-dependent contact nucleation and detachment mechanisms. Results identify an operating range in which contact recruitment and retained adhesive capacity are favorably balanced. The framework therefore provides an efficient tool for screening fibril geometries and operating conditions and for identifying adhesion windows governed by roughness, preload, and structural instability in reusable dry-adhesive interfaces.

title: Homogenization of one-dimensional periodic rod networks as special Cosserat rods
abstract: One-dimensional periodic rod networks are the structures that are obtained by periodically assembling its microstructural unit, a network of rods itself, in just one direction. In this work, we present a scheme for obtaining the nonlinear constitutive response of such structures when homogenized macroscopically as a continuum rod. To accurately capture arbitrary and large deformations, the geometrically exact special Cosserat rod theory is used for modeling the rod at both micro- and macroscales. By assuming the periodic structure to be strained uniformly, at macroscale, along its arc length, the full structure problem is reduced to just that of its microstructural unit but subjected to helically periodic boundary condition. The microscale problem, consisting of a network of rods and formulated in a variational setting, is solved in the presence of rod-joint constraints and helically periodic boundary conditions. The expressions for the macroscale rod’s stress resultants, i.e. internal contact force and moment, and stiffnesses are then obtained. Finally, several numerical examples having different microstructural units are presented to demonstrate our method. First, the results corresponding to simpler square and cross microstructural units are presented and validated with the existing literature. Square microstructural units having helical constituent rods are then taken up which have application as artificial muscle fiber material. Eventually, homogenization of auxetic tubular metamaterials is performed. It is shown how various design parameters of these microstructural units can be tuned to obtain the desired macroscopic response.

title: A model order reduction method of transient topology optimization for non-viscously damped systems
abstract: In this paper, an efficient model order reduction method for transient topology optimization of non-viscously damped system is developed. The damping force of the non-viscously damped system depends on the past motion history through convolution integrals with suitable kernel functions. The topology optimization problem is formulated to minimize the mean dynamic compliance, subject to a prescribed volume fraction constraint, with elemental relative densities as design variables. The time domain equations of motion are first constructed and a low dimensional projection basis is constructed via the multi-model method to reduce the dimension of the original system. Then, the equations are transformed into a state-space formulation to eliminate the convolution term. Within this reduced state-space system, the transient responses are computed using a modified precise integration method, followed by a differentiate-then-discretize adjoint variable method for design sensitivity analysis, and the design variables are updated using the method of moving asymptotes. The optimized designs, computational efficiency, relative error and implementation effort for topology optimization are discussed. Several 2D and 3D numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of the proposed method. The results show that the proposed framework provides a practical and robust tool for large scale transient topology optimization of non-viscously damped systems, enabling significant time savings without compromising solution quality.

title: Autoencoder-based non-intrusive model order reduction for anisotropic and multi-physics problems
abstract: Abstract We propose a non-intrusive, Autoencoder-based framework for reduced-order modeling in continuum mechanics. Our method integrates three stages: (i) an unsupervised Autoencoder compresses high-dimensional finite element solutions into a compact latent space, (ii) a supervised regression network maps problem parameters to latent codes, and (iii) an end-to-end surrogate reconstructs full-field solutions directly from input parameters. To overcome limitations of existing approaches, we propose two key extensions: a force-augmented variant that jointly predicts displacement fields and reaction forces at Neumann boundaries, and a multi-field architecture that enables coupled field predictions, such as in thermo-mechanical systems. The framework is validated on nonlinear benchmark problems involving heterogeneous composites, anisotropic elasticity with geometric variation, and thermo-mechanical coupling. Across all cases, it achieves accurate reconstructions of high-fidelity solutions while remaining fully non-intrusive. These results highlight the potential of combining deep learning with dimensionality reduction to build efficient and extensible surrogate models.

title: Splinenet: an isogeometric deep learning method for complex shells
abstract: We present a novel isogeometric deep learning method, termed SplineNet , for the seamless design and analysis of shell structures with complex geometries. The proposed approach is built upon watertight spline representations, analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines, and features exact geometric descriptions of computer-aided design (CAD) models in neural networks. Bézier extraction is used to build the network architecture, where Bernstein polynomials serve as the nonlinear activation functions. SplineNet can be applied in a data-free or data-driven way. In the data-free case, energy-based formulations can be naturally incorporated as loss terms, which fulfill the need of computer-aided engineering (CAE) and can be accurately calculated. In particular, the Kirchhoff–Love model is adopted to solve for the mechanical behaviors of shell structures. This way, CAD and CAE can be tightly integrated in a deep neural network without the time-consuming model/data exchange process. In the data-driven case, SplineNet can be used as the trunk net of deep operator networks to provide interpretability. Given such a trained network and unseen input data, results can be immediately obtained without retraining the network or repeatedly performing the traditional workflow for analysis. In the end, a variety of numerical examples are studied to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, especially when real-world complex geometries are involved. Comparisons with baseline models demonstrate the benefits of the spline representation in both solution learning and operator learning. The proposed method achieves lower relative \(L^2\) and \(H^1\) seminorm errors, together with shorter training time for operator learning. Incorporating derivative supervision further reduces the \(H^1\) seminorm errors and improves the relative \(L^2\) results.

title: An efficient proper generalized decomposition framework with high-order absorbing boundaries for 3D viscoelastic seismic wave modeling
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) viscoelastic wave modeling is essential in seismic applications, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive as domain size and simulation duration increase. To address this challenge, this study proposes a reduced-order modeling framework based on Proper Generalized Decomposition (PGD). A partially separated 2D + 1D representation decomposes the original 3D problem into coupled lower-dimensional subproblems. A high-order absorbing boundary condition based on the multi-transmitting formula (MTF) is embedded into the PGD framework, together with a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based recompression strategy that preserves the low-rank structure. Viscoelastic attenuation and point moment-tensor seismic sources are also incorporated. Numerical experiments are conducted on elastic full-space and half-space benchmarks, viscoelastic media spanning quality factors from purely elastic to strongly attenuating, multiple moment-tensor source mechanisms, and a horizontally layered half-space. The results demonstrate that the PGD-MTF effectively suppresses spurious boundary reflections and accurately reproduces the tested 3D wavefields in homogeneous and horizontally layered media. Performance benchmarks against the conventional spectral element method show that runtime and memory consumption are consistently reduced on the same benchmark mesh, with the gain depending on the scaling pattern. For the volume-scaling scenario at the largest tested mesh, the runtime speedup reaches 17.28, while the memory consumption is reduced by a factor of 33.98. Out-of-plane scaling further amplifies the advantage because it best matches the separated representation. The gain grows monotonically with problem size, indicating that PGD-MTF is an efficient and scalable tool for large-scale 3D seismic wave simulations in settings compatible with the adopted separated representation.

title: Generative design of funicular shells via physics-guided diffusion
abstract: Abstract Funicular shells carry loads predominantly through membrane action, achieving high structural efficiency with little material. Their computational design is difficult: the space of feasible forms is large, and classical optimisation explores it through local, problem-specific searches. Diffusion models offer an alternative by sampling from a learned distribution of plausible geometries, but coupling them with structural constraints is challenging, because physical guidance must act on noisy intermediate states whereas continuum-mechanical operators are defined on smooth geometries. Evaluating a non-linear shell operator on a denoised point estimate therefore yields a response that differs from the conditional mechanical response of the current diffusion state. We propose a modular two-branch Architect–Engineer pipeline. The Architect is a velocity-parameterised denoising diffusion model that learns an unconditional geometric prior over shell elevation maps. The Engineer is a time-conditioned Physics-Based Parallel UNet surrogate trained directly on noisy diffusion states, so that it predicts the mechanical response associated with the states visited during reverse sampling. The two models are trained independently and coupled only at inference, through a differentiable Membrane-Factor guidance pathway modulated by a bell-shaped schedule that concentrates the correction in the mid reverse process. On a dataset of funicular shells, the guided sampler raises the mean predicted Membrane Factor from 0.67 to 0.96, with 89% of samples above the 0.90 high-funicularity threshold, while preserving more geometric diversity than constant guidance. A guidance-strength sweep reveals a smooth transition between diversity-preserving and quality-prioritising regimes without architectural or training changes.

title: Collagen and myocyte interplay in cardiac volume overload: a multi-constituent growth and remodeling framework
abstract: Abstract Hearts subjected to volume overload (VO) are prone to detrimental anatomical and functional changes in response to elevated mechanical loading, ultimately leading to heart failure. Experimental findings now emphasize that organ-scale changes following VO cannot be explained by myocyte growth alone, as traditionally proposed in the literature. Collagen degradation, in particular, has been associated with VO and assumed to play a central role in both its acute and chronic stages. This hypothesis, however, remains to be substantiated by comprehensive mechanistic evidence, and each constituent contribution to myocardial growth and remodeling (G&R) processes is yet to be quantified. In this work, we present a multi-constituent G&R framework that integrates a mixture-based constitutive model within the kinematic growth formulation. This framework enables us to mechanistically assess the relative contributions of collagen and myocyte changes to alterations in tissue properties, ventricular dimensions, and growth phenotype. Our numerical results confirm that collagen remodeling affects the passive mechanical response of the myocardium, whereas myocytes predominantly influence the extent and phenotype of VO-induced growth. Importantly, collagen degradation exacerbates myocyte hypertrophy, revealing a synergistic interplay that accelerates the left ventricular eccentric growth and thereby promotes systolic dysfunction. This work constitutes an important step towards an integrated characterization of the early compensatory stages of VO-induced cardiac G&R.

title: Topology optimization for geometrically nonlinear structures with process-induced anisotropy
abstract: In the development of topology optimization methods for Additive Manufacturing (AM), accounting for the AM process-induced anisotropy of fabricated materials and the large deformations of slender members constitutes two significant engineering challenges. This paper proposes a novel structural topology optimization method that concurrently considers both effects. Firstly, the method introduces the print-off angle as an additional design variable, extending the orthotropic material model to characterize the anisotropic properties of AM-formed materials. Then, based on the finite deformation theory, the geometrically nonlinear mechanical behavior is simulated using the total Lagrangian formulation. The process-induced anisotropic constitutive relation is embedded into the geometrically nonlinear finite element equations, forming a coupled mechanical analysis framework that combines these two aspects. Furthermore, the Newton–Raphson method is applied to satisfy equilibrium conditions under large deformations. Additionally, numerical techniques, including density filtering, threshold projection, and adaptive control of the angular variable’s feasible domain, are integrated into the optimization process to stabilize the iterations. Finally, to enable efficient solutions via gradient-based optimization algorithms, sensitivity analyses with respect to both density and angle variables are derived in detail. Representative numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and reveal characteristic features of the optimized designs. The results show that the process-induced anisotropy can influence geometrically nonlinear design, with its effect tending to intensify as anisotropy deepens. The extent of this influence, however, appears to be problem-dependent. Optimizing the printing direction may offer performance benefits, particularly when design conditions are complex.

title: Lower-bound shakedown analysis of mixed-dimensional shell-solid structures using virtual node-based RBF coupling
abstract: Assessing the shakedown capacity of large-scale thin-walled structures under cyclic loading is essential for ensuring their long-term service safety. Existing direct shakedown methods are mostly based on a single type of finite element discretization, which leads to a persistent trade-off between computational efficiency and local accuracy for large-scale engineering structures: full solid models involve a prohibitive number of degrees of freedom, whereas pure shell models cannot adequately capture local three-dimensional stress gradients in regions such as joints and nozzle-shell intersections. To address this issue, this study proposes a lower-bound direct shakedown analysis framework for mixed-dimensional shell-solid structures according to which the linearized virtual nodes are constructed on the shell side, and an interface kinematic mapping matrix is established using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. The corresponding static equilibrium conditions are derived from the principle of virtual work so as to accurately transfer generalized forces and moments across the interface. For the yield conditions, the von Mises criterion in the solid subdomain and the Ilyushin criterion in the shell subdomain are adopted. Both of them are formulated into standard second-order cone constraints, leading to a mixed-dimensional second-order cone programming (SOCP) model. The proposed method is systematically validated using a square plate with a hole, a three-dimensional pipe joint, and a pressure vessel with a nozzle. The results show that the shakedown limits predicted by the hybrid models agree well with those of full solid benchmarks, demonstrating the accuracy and engineering applicability of the proposed method. The framework provides an efficient and accurate analysis tool for shakedown assessment of large-scale thin-walled structures.

title: Third medium contact in the finite cell method
abstract: Abstract Modelling of contact in the finite cell method (FCM) has been challenging due to immersed boundaries. Traditional approaches known from finite element methods (FEM) are not straight forward to use in immersed finite element methods, since explicit boundary descriptions are usually needed. A simple approach to introduce contact is the third medium contact (TMC) formulation, where the void domain is filled with a soft material which acts as a barrier between possible contact pairs. In the present work, we apply the TMC to the FCM by using a local enrichment strategy. By doing so, the weak discontinuity induced by the material interface to the third medium can be resolved. Various numerical examples show, that the combination of TMC and FCM and local enrichment opens the field for further research into contact formulations using TMC and the FCM.

title: A hybrid model–data framework for elastoplasticity with kinematic and isotropic hardening
abstract: Abstract Data-driven computational mechanics offers an alternative solution methodology to conventional methods by replacing constitutive models with data spaces defining admissible material states. Originally proposed for linear elasticity, its application to plasticity remains challenging. Purely data-driven plasticity schemes are usually restricted to one-dimensional problems due to the excessively large data space required as a result of path dependence. Hybrid frameworks combining constitutive assumptions with data have shown promise but are often limited by their underlying assumptions such as isotropic hardening or their inability to capture strain-path changes. In this work, a new hybrid model–data plasticity framework is proposed that incorporates kinematic and isotropic hardening via data spaces derived from discrete datasets, while adopting Prager’s law for back stress evolution without explicitly defining its functional form. The approach preserves the standard computational plasticity algorithmic procedures, while an implicit return-mapping procedure and a search direction calculation akin to the elastoplastic tangent are performed through the data spaces. Numerical examples in one and three-dimensional problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in more general plasticity problems.

title: A pole-residue polynomial-chaos neural network for stochastic frequency response of MDOF systems
abstract: Abstract The statistics of the frequency response of an uncertain structure are most demanding to compute near lightly damped resonances. As the parameters vary, the resonant frequencies migrate, so at a fixed frequency the response depends sharply on the parameters, and a polynomial surrogate converges slowly there. We propose to work on its partial-fraction representation characterized by poles and residues. The surrogate is an encoder–decoder with a physical bottleneck, in which an encoder maps the random parameters into the spectral data and a fixed analytic pole–residue layer decodes them into the response. We introduce two encoders of the spectral data, a direct polynomial-chaos map, PR-PCE, and a neural-network encoder that takes the chaos basis as its feature map, PR-PCNN. We develop the construction for a random vector indexed by the frequency. A complementary route learns the same spectral code from sampled responses alone, independently of the system matrices. The framework is verified on two systems, a three-degree-of-freedom structure and a clamped–free beam whose flexural rigidity is a random field. On both, the linear PR-PCE map is the most accurate, the neural encoders follow it, and a frequency-wise chaos expansion trails them. The representation is also benchmarked against a stochastic frequency transformation and a per-realisation vector fit. For these smooth spectral data the linear map stays the more accurate, and the value of the neural encoder lies in its flexibility, since it also learns the code end-to-end and from sampled responses alone.
